text: A company's HR scoped application has an employee table with a salary_band field. General HR staff need most of the record for day-to-day casework; only a small compensation team should ever see salary_band. This lab wires up both the table-level and field-level ACLs and traces exactly how they combine.

Step one is the record-wide check. General HR staff carry an hr_user role, and a manager can also see their own direct reports' records. This ACL decides one thing only -- can this user open the employee record at all -- and says nothing yet about which individual fields they'll see once inside.

Step two is a second, narrower gate on salary_band specifically: only members of an hr_compensation group, or anyone holding an hr_compensation_admin role, pass. Notice this script never queries the group membership table directly -- isMemberOf reuses GlideUser's already-cached data. Checking membership this way is fast, and salary_band is exactly the kind of field read constantly across list views and reports, so getting this right actually matters.

Trace a user who holds hr_user but isn't in the compensation group. The table-level check passes -- they can open the record. The field-level check, evaluated in addition to that, not instead of it, comes back false, because neither the group check nor the role check succeeds. The result: the record is visible, but salary_band is simply absent. Passing the table-level ACL never substitutes for passing the field-level one.

A compensation-team member going through the same record passes both checks and sees salary_band populated normally -- same two ACLs, different outcome, driven entirely by group membership. Because the field-level script leans on isMemberOf instead of a manual query, this same check scales across hundreds of rows in a list view or a full scheduled report without multiplying database queries per row.

Correct behavior, independent gates, and a group-membership check that stays fast under load. That closes out Chapter 2. Next, Chapter 3 opens with local versus SSO authentication -- how a user proves who they are in the first place, before any ACL ever gets a chance to run.
